description: Around an Athenian meal, guests define love. Aristophanes tells of the androgynes, Socrates elevates desire towards Beauty. Plato transforms celebration into philosophy.

hero.hook: A very drunken evening. And suddenly, the most beautiful definition of love.

blocks.text: In Athens, in the **4th century BC**, **Plato**, Greek philosopher and disciple of Socrates, wrote the **Banquet**. In Greek, we say *Symposium*. The setting is a , a masculine after-dinner meal where diluted wine and intellectual discussions are mixed. That evening, the imposed theme is , the force that pushes the soul towards beauty. **[[Eros]]** [[Athenian Symposium]]

Each guest offers a theory of love. The dialogue becomes a climb: from the body to beauty, from beauty to **Ideas**, perfect and eternal forms according to Plato. And **Socrates**, Plato's master, condemned to death in 399, as often in Platonic dialogues, has the last word.

The banquet celebrates the victory of the poet **Agathon**, tragic author and host of the evening. The hangovers are still there, but we decide to praise Eros rather than drink too much. The speeches follow one another: doctors, poets, politicians. Everyone projects their vision of desire. **Phaedra** speaks of love as the driving force of courage. **Pausanias** distinguishes noble love and coarse love.

blocks.caption: The Greek symposion: wine, crowns and speech as social sport.

blocks.text: Plato uses the festival to do philosophy without lectures. We laugh, we provoke, we correct each other. The idea advances with the wine, but also thanks to the rules of the game: everyone must defend Eros in front of the others. The eloquence competition, the Greek *agon*, becomes a school of thought.

The most famous speech is that of **Aristophanes**, an Athenian comic author known for his satires. In the past, he said, humans were double-minded. The  mixed masculine and feminine characters. Other couples were united. **Zeus**, king of the gods, cut them in two to punish them. Since then, everyone has been looking for their lost half. [[androgynes]]
This story gave the French expression “soulmate”. Plato puts it in the mouth of a comedian, then goes beyond it: love does not stop at finding a lost body.

The myth is beautiful, tender, a little sad. It explains the **lack**, this feeling of incompleteness which pushes us to look for the other. But Socrates goes elsewhere: to love is not just to stick two halves together. It’s about rising towards something greater than yourself.

Socrates reports the teaching of **Diotima**, foreign priestess and figure of wisdom in the dialogue. Eros is neither a full god nor a poor mortal: he is a , an intermediary being between gods and men. He wants what he lacks. The lover starts from the beautiful body, moves on to beautiful souls, then to beautiful actions, until **Beautiful in oneself**, the perfect Idea of ​​beauty. [[daimon]]

blocks.caption: Socrates and Alcibiades: desire can also be a school of the soul.

blocks.text: It's the , a desire that educates. Later, , a young Athenian politician, handsome and unstable, drunk, bursts in and praises Socrates as a disturbing Satyr. Philosophical love does not abolish carnal disorder. He transforms it into a quest for truth. [[Platonic Eros]] [[Alcibiades]]

sections.title: Diotima and the scale of love

blocks.text: In common parlance, “platonic” love means without carnal relationships. In Plato, it is richer: the body is a starting point, not a shame. The Banquet left its mark on Christian theology, the love poetry of Petrarch or Ronsard, and the psychology of desire. It shows that to love is also to learn to see.
In the **Banquet**, Plato turns an Athenian evening into a scale: we start from sensitive desire to aim for a broader beauty. To love, here, is to learn to see beyond yourself.
